title: Evaluation of Cryobiopsy in the Colon: Quality of Obtained Samples, Depth of Penetration, and Optimal Freezing Time in Surgical Resection Specimens
summary:
Taking tissue samples with small forceps is currently the standard method to examine abnormalities in the colon. However, this usually only retrieves a very shallow layer of tissue—about half a millimeter to one millimeter deep. This makes it difficult for pathologists to assess important features, such as how deeply a tumor has invaded the tissue.

A modern alternative is called cryobiopsy. In this method, tissue is frozen using a special probe and then removed. This allows for deeper and better-preserved samples. The technique is already well established in lung medicine, where it can yield tissue samples up to 8 millimeters in size. In the gastrointestinal tract, however, it has only been studied to a limited extent so far.

Initial studies suggest that the method is also safe to use in the digestive tract. For example, one study showed that cryobiopsy through the esophagus into the mediastinum can be done safely without an increased risk of injury. The cryoprobe has also been successfully tested in the bile ducts, stomach, and liver—partly in animal studies.

So far, there have been no systematic studies to examine whether and how well cryobiopsy works in the colon. The aim of this study is therefore to assess for the first time whether the method is technically feasible, how deep the samples go, and what freezing time works best—compared directly to conventional forceps biopsy. These findings are intended to lay the groundwork for future clinical use.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Age ≥ 18 years
Elective colonic resection for colorectal carcinoma
Informed consent via Broad Consent for the use of biological samples
Exclusion criteria:
Tumor size < 2 cm in the resection specimen
Refusal of Broad Consent
